title: Tenant isolation: KV spill, batching circuit-breaker, and short-term oncall playbook (wip)
content:
Summary:

This is a working incident review + on-call playbook for a pattern we've observed in the last two months where a combination of aggressive prefetching, multi-tenant continuous batching, and delayed KV-cache compaction leads to transient host-level OOMs and degraded latency for best-effort tenants.

Why this doc exists:
- collect telemetry and root-cause hypotheses across multiple occurrences
- provide an emergency runbook for on-call SREs to reduce blast radius quickly
- capture mitigations and long-term design proposals (tenant isolation, kv-spill-to-disk, batching circuit-breaker)

Observed symptoms (recurring):
- hosts report gradual resident memory growth over ~20–40 minutes followed by sudden OOM kill of the runtime worker process (SIGKILL)
- request success rate for low-tier tenants drops during memory increase; tail latency spikes for all tenants on the host
- stack traces (when captured) show blocking on prefix prefetch operations and high number of open KV slab segments in in-memory index
- autoscaler reacts by throttling new hosts (eviction/scale-in flap) causing capacity oscillation

Key telemetry signals to watch (dashboards/alerts):
- host.resident_mb 95th/99th over 60m window (alert if > 90% of host memory for 3 consecutive mins)
- runtime.kv_index_entries and runtime.kv_prefetch_inflight by tenant (increase in prefetch_inflight per tenant correlates with growth)
- batch.queue_len and batch.batch_size_p95 per host (sudden drop in batch_size with residual queue indicates starvation)
- OOM kills per host (count) and coredump presence
- per-tenant p99 latency and error-rate spikes

Representative timeline from incident RED-3821 (abridged):
- 09:02: initial small spike in prefetch_inflight for Tenant X after new workload rollout (long context prompts)
- 09:10: host.resident_mb starts increasing steadily; KV index entries up 3x baseline on same host
- 09:25: batch.batch_size_p50 drops, backlog appears, average latency increases
- 09:32: kernel OOM-killer terminates runtime worker; host removed from pool; autoscaler launches replacement host but capacity dip causes queued requests to retry/fallback
- 09:45: services recover after restarts and tenant revert

Hypothesis (root cause):
- Confluence of factors: (1) prefetch depth logic allows aggressive growth of KV cache entries when clients send long prefixes repeatedly; (2) continuous-batching keeps requests alive waiting for larger batches which increases resident allocations for KV shards; (3) our KV-compact/eviction sampler is tuned for steady state and doesn't reclaim fast enough during bursts, leading to sustained resident memory growth and eventual host OOM.
- Tenant X's workload pattern (many parallel long-context requests with little reuse) creates KV churn and prevents effective prefix cache hits, amplifying memory consumption.

Immediate on-call playbook (urgent steps):
1) Identify impacted hosts
   - query hosts with runtime.kv_index_entries > tenant-specific threshold and resident_mb increasing 3-samples in a row
   - command examples: 
     - kubectl -n runtime get pods -l hostpool=shared -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name} {.status.containerStatuses[0].name} {.metrics.memory.usageBytes}{"\n"}{end}'
     - internal metric query: metrics("host.resident_mb{host=~\"host-.*\"}")
2) Apply emergency tenant-shed for the offending tenant
   - use routing dynconfig to mark Tenant X as degraded/limited: set tenant-routing.policy[TenantX]=fallback-light
   - if routing change not possible quickly, apply temporary qps limit at edge for Tenant X (rate-limit token buckets)
3) Disable aggressive prefetching globally (temporary):
   - flip dynconfig runtime.kv_prefetch.max_depth = 1 (from 8) for the affected region
   - note: this will increase cold-start latency for some workloads but prevents cache explosion
4) Toggle batching circuit-breaker (if available):
   - enable dynconfig: batch.circuit_breaker.enabled = true and set batch.circuit_breaker.max_inflight_per_host = 64
   - alternative: route heavy-tenants to dedicated pool if they exist
5) Drain affected hosts cleanly and restart runtime workers:
   - mark host as drain: kubectl annotate node/host-XXX maintenance=true
   - evict pods gracefully and let autoscaler replenish from reserved pool
6) Collect debug artifacts before restart (if possible):
   - /proc/<pid>/maps, heap profiles, runtime metrics snapshot (kv-index histogram), and runtime logs with debug=kv
   - upload to incident bucket with clear naming: s3://incidents/RED-3821/host-<id>/
7) Post-mitigation observation window (60 minutes)
   - watch resident_mb for regressions, per-tenant prefetch_inflight, p99 latencies

Safety/rollback notes:
- dynconfig flips are low risk but can affect latency; ensure communications to growth/solutions teams before flips beyond 15 minutes
- if enabling circuit-breaker causes increased 429s, have a fallback policy to route to lower latency model or reduce weight for heavy tenants

Longer-term mitigations and design proposals (owners assigned):
- Short-term (2–3 weeks):
  - implement tenant-scoped soft memory quotas in the runtime (owner: Maya Rodriguez) — allow per-tenant kv_index cap and graceful spill-to-disk when exceeded
  - improve KV compaction heuristics for bursty workloads (owner: Ethan Brooks) — detect sustained growth and accelerate sampler frequency
  - add per-tenant prefetch budgets and backpressure signals to router (owner: Lin Zhao)
- Medium-term (1–3 months):
  - prototype async KV-spill-to-disk for cold prefixes (tradeoff: read latency) and benchmark (owner: Serving Runtime team)
  - batching admission controller that enforces max inflight per tenant and drops/bypasses when there is memory pressure (owner: Platform Engineering)
  - better telemetry: per-tenant resident estimate and per-tenant heap-slices in host metrics (owner: Observability)
- Long-term (quarter+):
  - consider tenant placement policies and dedicated pools for heavy-tenants based on historical footprint
  - explore kernel-level cgroup improvements for more deterministic OOM handling and earlier eviction triggers

Open questions / unresolved items:
- What is the acceptable SLA tradeoff for disabled prefetch? Need product input (cc product-hosted-api).
- How often does prefetch growth correlate with non-KV allocations (model activations)? We need deeper heap profiling to separate KV vs other allocs.
- Do any tenants intentionally rely on our old prefetch semantics (possible breakage)? Add a canary before global flips.

Immediate follow-ups (tickets to make):
- Follow-up P1: RED-3821 (already created) - postmortem and telemetry gaps
- Follow-up P2: RED-3890 - implement tenant soft quotas for kv-cache (owner: Maya)
- Follow-up P3: RED-3891 - batching circuit-breaker feature flag and integration test (owner: Lin)

Playbook checklist (quick):
- [ ] Identify hosts and tenants (metrics + logs)
- [ ] Apply tenant routing/edge qps limit
- [ ] Flip prefetch max_depth -> 1 (dynconfig)
- [ ] Enable batching circuit-breaker
- [ ] Drain and restart impacted hosts after artifact collection
- [ ] Monitor for 60m and reopen if memory climbs

Notes to oncaller (voice):
- If you hit a live OOM spike, prioritize limiting the offending tenant rather than immediately restarting many hosts — restarts can make capacity oscillation worse.
- When collecting heap/profile data, aim to secure it quickly; large profiles may fail upload if host is close to OOM.

Appendix: useful commands / queries
- find hosts with rising resident memory (pseudo):
  metrics_query 'max_over_time(host.resident_mb[5m]) - min_over_time(host.resident_mb[5m]) > 200MB and node_role==runtime'
- dump kv index histogram (on host):
  sudo /usr/local/bin/runtime-inspect --dump-kv-histogram > /tmp/kv-histogram.json
- temporarily throttle tenant at edge (kong / gateway example):
  curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer $ADMIN' https://gateway.internal/tenants/TenantX/limits -d '{"qps": 5}'

Owners and contacts:
- Incident owner: Avery Patel (eng-sre)
- Runtime vm and KV owner: Ethan Brooks (serving-runtime)
- Prefetch and router owner: Lin Zhao (platform-engineering)
- Observability dashboards: Maya Rodriguez (observability)
